title: 1 John
subtitle: God is light, God is love, and the life could be touched
lead: 1 John is a letter without a greeting, a name or an address. It opens like the Gospel of John, with "the beginning" and with eyewitnesses who heard, saw and touched "the word of life", and it closes with a sudden warning against idols. In between it circles around a few great themes again and again: God is light, God is love, Jesus Christ has come in the flesh, and those born from God show it by keeping his commands and loving each other.

It was written to churches that had just been split. A group had "gone out from us" (2:19), denying that Jesus is the Messiah who came in the flesh, and the letter calls them antichrists. Its purpose is to steady those who stayed: "so that you will know that you have eternal life" (5:13). Its sayings, "God is love", "complete love throws fear out", "we love because he loved us first", have become some of the best known in the Bible.
facts: The letter names no author. Traditionally John the apostle, the son of Zebedee; many scholars think of John the Elder or another member of a circle of John's disciples. See the authorship table.
Uncertain; often placed late in the first century, after the Gospel of John. Wikipedia's article on the letter gives "probably written in Ephesus between 95 and 110 AD".
Not stated. Tradition links John with Ephesus, in the Roman province of Asia (Irenaeus; Eusebius).
Churches the letter does not name, shaken by the departure of a group (2:19) whom it calls antichrists (2:18-22).
A circular letter or written sermon: no greeting, no farewell, a spiraling argument built on contrasts (light and darkness, truth and lie, love and hate).
Greek, in a simple style with a small vocabulary
The Gospel of John (shared words and ideas throughout); 2 and 3 John (the same circle, probably the same writer)
authorship: The apostle John, the disciple whom Jesus loved, wrote the letter late in life at Ephesus, as he wrote the Gospel. Irenaeus (about 180) quotes it as the letter of John, "the disciple of the Lord", and Eusebius counts "the former of his epistles" among the books "accepted without dispute" (Church History 3.24.17).

Eusebius quotes Papias, who named two Johns, the apostle and "the presbyter John", and reports that there were "two tombs in Ephesus, each of which ... is called John's" (Church History 3.39.5-7). Some scholars think the Elder of 2 John 1 and 3 John 1 wrote all three letters; Martin Hengel argued that John the Elder wrote the Gospel and the letters, and Richard Bauckham that he wrote the Gospel.
A circle or school of John's disciples

The letter's "we" (1:1-4) may be a group of teachers who kept the eyewitness tradition. Most critical scholars conclude that John the apostle did not write the Johannine works, and there is no scholarly consensus on who did.

Most scholars think the three letters have the same author, but there is no consensus that he also wrote the Gospel. Heinrich Holtzmann and C. H. Dodd judged the Gospel and 1 John to be by different authors; Ernest DeWitt Burton saw "no reasonable doubt" that they share an author. Most scholars agree that one borrows directly from the other.

audience.to: Christians in a circle of house churches that the letter never names. Tradition places John at Ephesus, the great city of the Roman province of Asia. The letter itself shows rich and poor among them (3:17), traveling teachers and prophets (4:1; compare 2 John 10 and 3 John 5-10), and a recent split: some of their own members had gone out (2:19). It calls the one who denies that Jesus is the Messiah the liar and the antichrist (2:22), and says that every spirit that does not confess Jesus is not from God (4:2-3). Who the departed were, and what exactly they taught, has to be reconstructed from these few lines: see the views below.
audience.why: To steady the people who stayed. The writer reminds them of the eyewitness message they heard "from the beginning" (1:1-3; 2:24), gives them tests to tell true teaching and life from false (keeping God's commands, loving the brothers, confessing Jesus come in the flesh), calls the departed teachers "antichrists" and the readers God's children, and tells them plainly why he writes: "so that you will know that you have eternal life" (5:13). Knowing the split changes the reading. The letter's tender words about love are not general advice; they are spoken to a wounded church, and its hard words about liars and the devil's children are aimed at people who had walked out, not at outsiders, and not at Jews.
views: The opponents held that Christ only seemed to have a body, the teaching Ignatius of Antioch opposed in those who said he "only seemed to suffer" (To the Smyrnaeans 2), and which Polycarp answered with this letter's words (Philippians 7); hence the stress on flesh and blood (4:2; 5:6).

The opponents taught, as Irenaeus reports of Cerinthus, that the Christ came on Jesus at his baptism and "at last Christ departed from Jesus" (Against Heresies 1.26.1); Irenaeus quotes 2:18-22 against the systems "which divide the Lord" (3.16.5).

Raymond Brown: both sides knew the teaching of the Fourth Gospel, and they "interpret it differently" (The Community of the Beloved Disciple, 1979); they split over Christ, ethics, the last things and the Spirit.
Jewish believers going back to Judaism

Terry Griffith: reading 2:22 as "The Messiah is Jesus", he holds that "it is the messiahship of Jesus that is in question", and the letter deals with Jewish Christians returning to Judaism; 4:2 restates 2:22, and the warning against idols (5:21) turns Jewish polemic back on Judaism (Tyndale Bulletin 48.1, 1997).
The letter is a sermon for several churches, with the split as one occasion among others, and its tests are meant for every reader.

outline: The opening: what we heard, saw and touched
God is light; walking in the light; confessing sin; the Advocate
Knowing him means keeping his commands; the old and new command
Why I am writing; do not love the world
The last hour: antichrists and the anointing
God's children: born from God, they do not sin
Love each other: Cain, the cross and the needy brother
Faith that wins the victory; the three witnesses
So that you may know: prayer, the sin headed toward death, the real God, idols

lenses.name: History and setting
lenses.desc: Reads 1 John as a letter to real churches after a split: the group that "went out", what they taught (docetism, Cerinthus, or a Jewish denial that Jesus is the Messiah), house churches in the cities of Asia, traveling prophets, and the tradition of John at Ephesus.

lenses.name: Critical
lenses.desc: Asks who wrote it (the apostle, the Elder, a circle of John's disciples), how it relates to the Gospel and to 2 and 3 John, what kind of writing it is, when it was written, and what the manuscripts read, including the Johannine Comma and the ECM's text.

lenses.name: Literary
lenses.desc: Follows the letter's spiral form: themes that return and deepen, the "if we say" and "by this we know" lines, the contrasts of light and darkness, truth and lie, love and hate, the key verb "remain", and the abrupt opening and ending.

lenses.name: Jewish reading
lenses.desc: Reads the letter's Jewish world: light and darkness and the two spirits in the Dead Sea Scrolls, the Day of Atonement and confession of sin, Cain in Jewish tradition, the Torah's distinction between sins by mistake and sins "with a high hand", the new covenant of Jeremiah 31, and the warning against idols.

lenses.name: Church tradition
lenses.desc: How the churches have read it: Augustine's homilies on love, the debate over the extent of the atonement (2:2), Christian perfection (3:6-9; Wesley, Luther, Westminster, Trent), mortal and venial sin (5:16-17), the anointing and chrismation (2:20, 27), theosis and the vision of God (3:2), and the history of the Johannine Comma.

sections.b:
Do not look for a straight line of argument. The letter's thought "moves in circles", as one description puts it: light, love, belief and obedience come back again and again, each time from a slightly different angle. Read it slowly, and notice the repeated tests: "Here is how we know" (2:3, 5; 3:16, 19, 24; 4:2, 6, 13; 5:2). Notice too the small, heavy words: menō, "remain" (24 times), "know" (25 times), "love" as noun and verb (46 times), "world" (23 times).

The letter has no greeting and no farewell. It may have been a written sermon or a circular for several house churches, carried and read aloud. Its style is simple Greek, with short clauses set side by side without joining words.

sections.h: 1 John and the Gospel of John
sections.b:
The letter shares the Gospel's vocabulary on nearly every line: light and darkness, truth, the world, remaining, the new command to love each other, the Advocate, being born from God, eternal life, "from the beginning". This site translates the letter with the Gospel's Plain wording wherever the Greek is the same, so that a reader can hear the echoes: "so that our joy will be filled up" (1:4; John 16:24), "moved out of death and into life" (3:14; John 5:24), "the Savior of the world" (4:14; John 4:42), "his only Son" (4:9; John 3:16).

There are differences too. In the Gospel the Advocate is the Spirit; in the letter it is Jesus (2:1). The letter uses the word parousia for Christ's "coming" (2:28) and speaks of "the last hour" (2:18); neither expression is in the Gospel, though the Gospel too has Jesus promise, "I am coming again" (John 14:3), and speak of "the last day" (John 6:40). Many readers think the letter was written after the Gospel, to apply it to a church in which some were reading it wrongly; others think the letter came first.

sections.h: The early church and the canon
sections.b:
1 John was known early and never seriously doubted. Polycarp of Smyrna echoes it ("For whosoever does not confess that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh, is antichrist", Philippians 7). Eusebius reports that Papias "uses testimonies from the first Epistle of John" (Church History 3.39.16). Irenaeus quotes 2:18-22, 4:1-3 and 5:1 as John's (Against Heresies 3.16.5, 8). Clement of Alexandria quotes 5:16-17 from John's "larger Epistle" (Stromata 2.15), which shows that he knew a shorter one as well. The Muratorian list speaks of John's "epistles", and quotes the opening words.

Eusebius counts "the former epistle of John" among the books acknowledged by all, while "the second and third of John" were disputed (Church History 3.24.17; 3.25.2-3). Every church today receives all three.

The oldest piece of 1 John is Papyrus 9, a single crude leaf from Oxyrhynchus in Egypt, from the 200s, with parts of 4:11-17. The whole letter is in the great codices Vaticanus and Sinaiticus (300s) and Alexandrinus (400s). The Editio Critica Maior, a full edition of the Greek manuscripts of the Catholic Letters, published 1 John in 2003, and its second edition supplies the text of NA28 for these letters; NA28 changed the text of 1 John in four places from NA27 (1:7, 3:7, 5:10, 5:18). This site follows SBLGNT, weighing NA28/ECM where they differ, and gives every variant that changes the English or makes the KJV read differently, among them the famous "three heavenly witnesses" of the KJV's 5:7 (see the deep dive on chapter 5).

The letter's language is sharp: liars, antichrists, children of the devil. These words were aimed at members who had left a particular church over who Jesus is. They were not written about Jews, and they do not license treating anyone with contempt: the same letter says that "Everyone who hates his brother is a killer" (3:15). Christians who use the letter's tests on others have to use them first on themselves, as the letter's "we" does (1:6-10).

spec.title: Claude's theory: 1 John as a letter built on the Last Supper
spec.body: Many of the key words of 1 John also stand in the Last Supper discourse of John 13-17: "little children" (John 13:33), the "new command" to love each other (John 13:34), the Advocate (John 14:16), keeping his commands (John 14:15), remaining in him (John 15:4), the world's hatred (John 15:18), joy "filled up" (John 16:24), asking and receiving (John 16:24), "I have won the victory over the world" (John 16:33), keeping safe "from the evil one" (John 17:15) and "the only real God" (John 17:3). The letter may be the farewell discourse turned into a pastoral letter: the writer speaking to his "little children" the way Jesus spoke to his on the last night. That the letter shares the Gospel's language is plain (see "1 John and the Gospel of John" above); the suggestion that it is modeled on the farewell discourse in particular is Claude's theory. It does not explain everything: light and darkness, the antichrist, the anointing, the atoning sacrifice, "seed" and "lawlessness" do not come from John 13-17.

prompts: A sketch on aged parchment of several hands reaching toward a glowing figure whose outline is drawn in simple cave-painting lines; around them, faint Greek letters of 'what we heard, saw and touched'; warm ochre, charcoal and gold, soft torn edges, no hard frame.

A scroll-style drawing split by a soft diagonal: on one side a lamp flame drawn in loose ink washes, on the other side dark charcoal smudges thinning to nothing as the light spreads; small figures walking toward the light; modern brushwork mixed with ancient manuscript texture, rounded fading edges.

An ink-and-wash sketch of three simple symbols drawn as on a cave wall, a dove's wing, a stream of water and a red drop, joined by one thin line; marginal notes in faded Latin and Greek around them, as on an old manuscript page; soft vignette edges.
